1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.

1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.

1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?

1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map

1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.

1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:

1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles

1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.

1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.

1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)

1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*

1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.

1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:

1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.

1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
